questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line Through Two Points
questions.problem: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(0,-3)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(1,7)$ and $(-5,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes which are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,7)$ and $(-5,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-7}{-5-1} \\  & =\frac{-8}{-6} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{4}{3})=-1\,⇒\,m=-\frac{3}{4}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(0,-3).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-3) & =-\frac{3}{4}(x-0) \\ y+3 & =-\frac{3}{4}x \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line in Standard Form
questions.problem: Find the equation of the line that passes through the point $(5,1)$ and is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(1,5)$ and $(-3,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes which are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,5)$ and $(-3,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-5}{-3-1} \\  & =\frac{-6}{-4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{3}{2})=-1\,⇒\,m=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(5,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-5) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{10}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we want to write the equation in standard form. So, we will bring the $x$ term to the left-hand side and multiply both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{13}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}x+y & =\frac{13}{3} \\ 3\cdot (\frac{2}{3}x+y) & =3\cdot \frac{13}{3} \\ 2x+3y & =13\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line Through Two Points
questions.worked_solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(-4,-3)$ and $(2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{3-(-3)}{2-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{6}{6} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (1)=-1\,⇒\,m=-1.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(-5,5).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =-1(x-(-5)) \\ y-5 & =-1(x+5) \\ y-5 & =-x-5 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line Through Two Points
questions.worked_solution:
Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other.

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,-3)$ and $(3,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{4-(-3)}{3-1} \\  & =\frac{4+3}{3-1} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want a perpendicular line, the slope $m$ of the line we're trying to find must satisfy

$$
m\cdot (\frac{7}{2})=-1\,⇒\,m=-\frac{2}{7}.
$$

We know that the line passes through the point $(0,-5).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-5) & =-\frac{2}{7}(x-0) \\ y+5 & =-\frac{2}{7}x \\ y & =-\frac{2}{7}x-5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Line in Standard Form
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation $4x-3y=7$ in its slope-intercept form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-3y & =7 \\ -3y & =-4x+7 \\ y & =\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of the new line should be the negative reciprocal of the slope of the given line $y=\frac{4}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.$ The given line has a slope of $\frac{4}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\frac{3}{4}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\frac{3}{4}$ and pass through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(1,1).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{3}{4}(x-1) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{3}{4} \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
